id: A Wasp Woman Visits a Black Junkie in Prison

outputs.L1:
After explanations and regulations, he walked warily in. Black hair covered his chin, in keeping with a villainous ideal.

“This cannot be real,” he thought. “This is a classical mistake; this is a cake baked with embarrassing icing. Somebody has, likely as not, a big fat tongue in cheek. What have I to do with a prim and proper-blooded lady? Christ indeed has risen when a junkie in prison visits with a WASP woman.

“Hold your stupid face, man. Learn a little grace, man. Lower the sacred shield a notch. She might have good reason—like, ‘I was in prison and ye visited me not,’ or some such. So sweep clear anachronistic fear, fight the fog, and use no hot words.”

After the seating and the greeting, they fished for a denominator, common or uncommon, and could summon up only the fact that both were human.

“Be at ease, man. Try to please, man—the lady is as lost as you.”

“You got children, ma’am?” he said aloud.

The thrust broke the dam, and their lines wiggled in the water. She offered no pills to cure his many ills, no compact sermons, but small and funny talk: “My baby began to walk... simply cannot keep his room clean...”

Her chatter sparked no resurrection, and truly no shackles were shaken. But after she had taken her leave, he walked softly, and for hours used no hot words.
outputs.L2:
After receiving instructions and hearing the rules, he stepped inside cautiously. Dark hair covered his jaw, fitting the image of a dangerous man.  

“This cannot be happening,” he told himself. “This is some absurd, old-fashioned error—like a cake ruined by ridiculous frosting. Someone must be joking, probably with a huge tongue in their cheek. What business do I have with a stiff, respectable, well-bred lady?”  

It seemed almost miraculous: a prisoner with a drug habit being visited by a white Anglo-Saxon Protestant woman.  

“Control that foolish expression,” he told himself. “Show a little manners. Lower your defenses. She may have a real reason for coming—something like, ‘I was in prison, and you did not visit me,’ or whatever the saying is. So clear away these outdated fears, push through the confusion, and don’t speak harshly.”  

Once they had sat down and exchanged greetings, they searched for something they shared—some common ground, or even uncommon ground—but all they could find was the simple fact that they were both human beings.  

“Relax,” he urged himself. “Try to be pleasant. The woman is just as uncertain as you are.”  

Then he said out loud, “Do you have children, ma’am?”  

That question broke the barrier between them, and the conversation began to move. She did not bring medicine to heal his many troubles, nor did she offer neat little religious lessons. Instead, she spoke in light, ordinary, amusing ways: “My baby has started walking... he simply will not keep his room clean...”  

Her casual talk did not bring about any grand transformation, and no chains truly fell away. But after she left, he moved quietly, and for several hours he did not speak in anger.
outputs.L3:
A wary prisoner enters the visiting room full of suspicion and unease. He has already decided, in part, what kind of person he expects to meet: a proper, upper-class woman, distant from his world and unlikely to understand anything about him. His thoughts are shaped by prejudice as much as by fear. He doubts her sincerity, questions her motives, and can hardly believe that someone like her would come to see someone like him without judgment or hidden purpose.

Yet, as the visit begins, he makes a private effort to control himself. He challenges himself to behave with grace, even if he feels defensive. He tries to put aside his fear and resentment, and he resolves not to speak harshly or give in to the anger that often rises in him. This restraint is not easy. Every word, every silence, carries the possibility of misunderstanding. Still, he wants to prove, if only to himself, that he can meet the moment with dignity.

At first, the conversation is awkward. The prisoner and the woman seem to come from entirely different worlds, and neither knows quite how to bridge the distance between them. Their manners, assumptions, and experiences do not match. For a while, the only thing they clearly share is their basic humanity: two people sitting across from each other, uncertain of what to say, aware of the gulf between them.

Then a simple question changes the tone of the visit. When the subject of children comes up, the conversation becomes more natural. It moves away from suspicion and social difference and into the ordinary details of personal life. They begin to speak not as symbols of class, guilt, charity, or judgment, but as people with memories, attachments, and human concerns. This small opening allows them to connect in a modest but genuine way.

The visit does not produce any dramatic transformation. The prisoner is not suddenly redeemed, nor are all his suspicions erased. But something in him is softened. He leaves the encounter calmer than he entered it, less sharp in his manner and less ready to strike out with words. The meeting’s importance lies in its quiet effect: for a short time, it allows him to practice patience, courtesy, and trust, and that small change remains with him afterward.
outputs.L4:
The prisoner sat on the edge of the narrow bed with his shoulders drawn up, as if he were trying to take up as little space as possible. The room was not quite a cell and not quite an office: a gray-walled visiting room with a scratched table, two plastic chairs, and a window too high to see out of. The air smelled faintly of disinfectant, old coffee, and damp coats. He had been told that someone from a church group was coming to see him, and from the moment he heard it, he had been suspicious.

He knew the type, or thought he did. They came in carrying soft voices and hard ideas. They asked whether you had found God, whether you were sorry, whether you wanted to be saved. They looked at your arms, your teeth, your prison shoes, and tried not to look disgusted. Then they went home feeling useful.

So when the woman entered, small and neat in a dark skirt and buttoned coat, with a little hat pinned carefully over her gray hair, he tightened his mouth and waited for the performance to begin. She carried a worn handbag in both hands. Her gloves were folded together like something from another age. Everything about her seemed orderly: her collar, her hair, the way she sat down across from him and placed her bag beside her chair.

“Good afternoon,” she said.

He nodded but did not answer.

“My name is Mrs. Ellis.”

He glanced at her, then away. “I didn’t ask for a visit.”

“No,” she said. “I know.”

That surprised him a little. He had expected her to say that everyone needed someone, or that the Lord had sent her. Instead she sat quietly, not smiling too much, not reaching across the table, not pretending they were already friends.

After a moment, she said, “If you would rather I left, I can leave.”

He looked at her properly then. Her face was pale and lined, but not severe. She seemed nervous, though she was trying not to show it. That made him less eager to be cruel.

“Doesn’t matter to me,” he said.

“Then perhaps I’ll stay a little while.”

Silence settled between them. He stared at the tabletop, where someone had carved initials into the plastic with a key or a nail. She looked at the same marks, as if they were both studying a map.

“Cold today,” she said at last.

He gave a short laugh. “That what you came to talk about?”

“I suppose it is a beginning.”

He shrugged. “Yeah. Cold.”

“Do they give you enough blankets?”

He looked up sharply, suspicious again. “Why?”

“I wondered.”

“Yeah. Enough.”

“That’s good.”

Another silence followed. It should have been unbearable, but somehow it was not. She did not fill it with advice. She did not ask what he had done, though of course she must have known something. She did not ask about the drugs, either, though the drugs were written into his face and hands and the restless tapping of his foot.

He found himself saying, “Food’s bad.”

A small expression crossed her face, almost a smile. “Institutional food usually is.”

“You been locked up?”

“No,” she said. “But I spent six weeks in hospital once. They boiled everything until it surrendered.”

He snorted despite himself.

Encouraged, she opened her handbag and took out a packet of mints. “I’m not sure if I’m allowed to offer you one.”

“You’re not.”

“Ah.” She put the packet back carefully. “Then I won’t.”

He could have mocked her for that, for obeying every little rule. Instead he noticed her hands. They were thin, veined, and slightly trembling. She saw him notice and folded them in her lap.

“You scared?” he asked.

“A little,” she admitted.

He leaned back. “Of me?”

“Of doing the wrong thing.”

That was not the answer he expected. He had been ready to resent her fear, but not her humility.

“You people always know what to do,” he said.

“You people?”

“Church people. Good people.”

She considered that. “I don’t always know. And I’m not as good as I look.”

He studied her prim coat, her polished shoes, the little cross at her throat. “You look pretty good.”

“My appearance is misleading.”

This time he laughed more openly, though it turned quickly into a cough. She waited until it passed.

“Are you sleeping?” she asked.

“Some.”

“That sounds like no.”

“It sounds like some.”

She nodded, accepting the correction. “All right. Some.”

Again, the quiet came. Outside the room, keys clattered and a man shouted down the corridor. The prisoner’s jaw tightened at the sound. The woman did not flinch dramatically. She only turned her head, listened, and then looked back at him.

“What do you do when you’re not here?” he asked suddenly.

“When I’m not visiting?”

“Yeah.”

“I live alone. I go to church. I help with the jumble sale. I make soup on Thursdays for the lunch program. I feed an ungrateful cat that belongs to my neighbor but prefers my kitchen.”

He pictured it: the tidy kitchen, the old woman opening a tin for a cat that did not belong to her. It seemed absurdly far from him. It also seemed, in some strange way, peaceful.

“What’s the cat’s name?”

“Percy.”

“Percy,” he repeated, amused. “That’s a stupid name for a cat.”

“It is. He seems proud of it.”

He looked down at his hands. The nails were bitten short. There were scars along his knuckles, some from fights, some from accidents he barely remembered. He had spent years being either numb or desperate. Ordinary conversation felt almost indecent, as though they were pretending he was not what he was.

But she was not pretending. That was what unsettled him. She knew he was in prison. She knew he was an addict. She knew, at least in outline, that his life had gone wrong in ways that could not be repaired by tea, cats, or talk about the weather. Yet she spoke to him as if he were still a person who might have opinions about soup and blankets.

“Why’d you come?” he asked.

She took a breath before answering. “Because someone once came to see my brother when he was in a bad way. I don’t know if it helped him. But he remembered it.”

“Was he on drugs?”

“Yes.”

“What happened to him?”

She looked at her folded hands. “He died.”

The prisoner felt the urge to say something hard, something that would push the moment away. Instead he said nothing.

“I’m sorry,” he muttered finally.

“Thank you.”

“Did the visit help?”

“I don’t know,” she said. “It didn’t save him, if that’s what you mean. But for one afternoon he was not entirely alone.”

He looked away toward the high window. There was only a square of white sky visible, dull and colorless.

“I don’t need saving,” he said.

“No,” she replied softly. “Perhaps not today.”

He bristled, then realized there had been no challenge in her voice. She was not arguing with him. She was simply leaving the door open, not pushing him through it.

The visit lasted twenty more minutes. They talked about small things: whether he liked to read, what the prison library had, how terrible instant coffee was, how long winter seemed after Christmas. She did not quote Scripture. She did not ask him to kneel. She did not promise that everything would be better if only he believed the right words. When she mentioned prayer, she did so only at the end, while standing with her handbag tucked under her arm.

“Would you mind if I prayed for you?” she asked.

He stiffened automatically. “Out loud?”

“No. Not unless you wanted me to.”

“I don’t.”

“Then I won’t.”

He nodded.

“But I may pray later?”

He looked at her, at the careful hope in her face and the equal care with which she hid it. “Do what you want.”

“I will,” she said.

At the door, she turned back. “May I come again?”

He wanted to say no. It was safer to say no. Visits made a man expect things, and expectation was dangerous. It led to disappointment, anger, need. He had spent a long time training himself not to need anyone who could walk away.

Instead he shrugged. “If they let you.”

“I’ll ask.”

After she left, the room seemed colder. He remained at the table until an officer told him to get up. Back in his cell, he lay on his bed and stared at the underside of the bunk above him. Nothing had changed. The door was still locked. His body still ached with the old hunger. His case was still his case, his past still his past. No light broke through the ceiling. No voice spoke from heaven. He did not become a different man.

But later, when the evening meal came and he found the potatoes as gray and tasteless as ever, he thought of her saying the hospital vegetables had been boiled until they surrendered. Against his will, he smiled.

It was a small thing. Almost nothing. A conversation about weather, blankets, cats, bad food, and sleep. Yet something in him had loosened, not enough to free him, but enough for him to notice the tightness that had been there before. She had not rescued him. She had not demanded gratitude. She had simply sat across from him without disgust, without hurry, and without trying to turn him into a lesson.

For that afternoon, he had not been only an addict, only a prisoner, only a ruined man in a gray room. He had been someone worth speaking to gently.

And though he would not have used the word himself, that gentleness was a form of compassion. It did not announce itself. It did not conquer. It did not transform his life in a single dramatic hour. But it reached him all the same, quietly and stubbornly, like warmth through a wall.
outputs.L5:
After the rain stopped, Mara walked down the quiet street beneath a sky still heavy with clouds. The pavement shone like glass, reflecting the pale glow of the streetlights. At the end of the road stood an old house with black shutters and a garden tangled with weeds.

She had passed it many times before, but tonight something felt different. A small black cat sat on the porch, watching her with bright green eyes. When Mara stepped closer, the cat stood, stretched, and slipped through the half-open gate.

Curious, she followed.

The garden was silent except for the sound of her footsteps on the wet path. After a few moments, the cat stopped beside a wooden box hidden under a bush. Mara lifted the lid and found a bundle of old letters tied with a faded ribbon.

She smiled softly, realizing she had discovered a forgotten piece of someone’s story. And as she walked home under the clearing sky, the black cat followed close behind.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse narrative poem about a hardened prisoner being visited by an upper-class Christian woman, with awkward social contrast, biblical allusions, and a small moment of human connection.
counterfactuals.output:
She came in wearing Sunday  
as if it were a clean white glove—  
hat pinned to her careful hair,  
pearls at her throat like little moons  
that had never seen a yard light flicker  
over razor wire.

The guard called her ma’am  
and opened doors for her  
with a softness he never used on us.

I watched her cross the visiting room,  
heels clicking on the concrete  
like a spoon against fine china,  
and I thought of all the places  
those shoes had been allowed to enter—  
parlors, vestibules, garden paths,  
the front pew under stained glass  
where Christ bled beautifully in red and blue.

She looked for me  
as though my face might be written  
on a seating card.

I almost laughed.

My hands were on the table,  
big, nicked, tattooed with names  
of men dead or missing,  
and one blue cross I got at nineteen  
because I was afraid of hell  
but not afraid enough  
of anything else.

She sat down across from me  
and placed her purse in her lap  
like a sleeping animal.

“Mr. Harlan?” she asked.

Nobody had called me Mister  
since the judge did it  
before giving me thirty years.

“Yes, ma’am,” I said,  
and the words came out rough,  
dragged up from some cellar  
where manners had been chained  
and forgotten.

She smiled too quickly.  
Her eyes moved once  
to the scar across my cheek,  
then returned to my eyes  
as if repenting.

“I’m from St. Mark’s,” she said.  
“We’ve been praying for the men here.”

The men here.  
As if we were weather.  
As if we were stones in a field.

I wanted to tell her prayer  
had never picked a lock,  
never paid a debt,  
never put a hand between my mother  
and my father’s fist.

But she opened a little Bible,  
leather-bound, gold-edged,  
the kind that looks less read  
than inherited.

She began with the thief on the cross—  
of course she did—  
the one who found paradise  
with nails through his wrists  
and no time left  
to disappoint anyone.

“Today,” she read,  
her voice trembling a little,  
“you will be with me in paradise.”

In the room around us  
men leaned toward wives,  
toward sisters,  
toward children growing tall  
behind smeared glass years.  
A baby cried.  
A vending machine hummed  
its mechanical psalm.

I said, “Lady, I ain’t asking for paradise.”

Her mouth closed.  
The Bible stayed open  
between us like a small door.

“What are you asking for?” she said.

That stopped me.

Nobody had asked me that  
without already holding a form,  
a sentence,  
a baton,  
a grudge.

I looked at her hands.  
Soft, yes—  
but not useless.  
There was a half-moon burn  
near her thumb,  
the kind a person gets  
from an oven rack  
when pulling bread out too fast.

I said, “Coffee that don’t taste like rust.”  
Then, because she laughed—  
one startled note,  
bright and wrong in that room—  
I laughed too.

It hurt my chest.

She covered her mouth, embarrassed,  
and for a second the pearls,  
the prison blues,  
the guard with his keys,  
the whole iron sermon of the place  
fell quiet.

She told me she burned biscuits  
every Christmas morning  
and her husband ate them anyway  
with too much jam.  
I told her my mother made cornbread  
in a black skillet  
and slapped my hand  
when I reached before grace.

“Did you say grace?” she asked.

“When she was watching.”

She smiled again,  
not the church smile,  
not the mercy smile,  
but one person seeing  
another person standing cold  
outside Eden  
with dirt on his knees.

Before she left,  
she did not touch me—  
rules were rules,  
and guards were guards—  
but she slid a wrapped peppermint  
across the table,  
contraband maybe,  
or communion.

“For the coffee,” she said.

I held it in my palm  
after she was gone,  
small and white and red,  
a little wheel of sweetness  
turning nowhere.

That night in my cell  
I thought of Lazarus,  
not the rich man’s beggar  
licked by dogs at the gate,  
but the other one—  
called out of the tomb  
still stinking of death,  
still tangled in his grave clothes,  
blinking hard  
at the terrible light.

I did not feel risen.

But I unwrapped the candy slowly,  
as if it were something sacred,  
and laid it on my tongue.

For one minute  
the dark had flavor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem in the style of a mid-century satirical religious poet, using capitalized abstract nouns, internal rhyme, and colloquial speech, about a junkie inmate meeting a prim WASP volunteer visitor.
counterfactuals.output:
**Visiting Hour**

He sat in State blues with a twitch in his shoes,  
a thin little grin for the Lady from Grace,  
while Mercy and Order, those clerks at the border,  
kept filing their nails in the visitors’ place.

She wore a small hat and a look that said *that*  
is a cigarette burn, and *this* is a soul;  
her gloves were as white as the bite of the light  
on the tiled, trial-mile of Correction’s bowl.

“Well, how do you do?” “Aw, I do like I do.  
You got any smokes?” “I’m afraid I have none.”  
Then Charity coughed, and Propriety doffed  
her sensible coat to the Prodigal Son.

He said, “Ma’am, the Lord? Yeah, I heard of that Board.  
They meet, and they pray, and they turn down your plea.  
If Heaven’s upstairs, tell ’em fix their damn stairs;  
I been climbing all night and they keep losing me.”

She blushed for his words, for the wardens, the birds,  
for the whole fallen zoo of the flesh and the street;  
but Pity, that snob, took a part-time job  
washing blood from the cuffs of Respectable feet.

“Addiction,” she said, “is a sickness.” His head  
made a nod like a coin going down in a slot.  
“Sure, ma’am, and Sin is the skin that I’m in,  
and I scratch it for God knows precisely what.”

The clock with its face, like Institutional Grace,  
looked down and pronounced that the human was late.  
Two hands took a minute to diminish the visit;  
Hope signed the form and was shown to the gate.

“God bless you,” she whispered. “He might,” said the prisoner.  
“He’s got a good heart, though He runs with a crowd.”  
Then Faith, prim and shaken, went out to her station,  
and Love, in the hallway, laughed much too loud.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary parody poem where a suspicious ex-con or prisoner expects hypocrisy from a “proper” lady visitor but is softened by ordinary conversation about children.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Visitor in Grey Gloves**

I knew her sort before she came—  
The bonnet, book, and eyes cast down;  
A lady from the better streets  
To pity rogues from better town.

She’d bring, thought I, a polished text,  
A sermon folded neat and small,  
And look at me as if my sins  
Had stained the whitewash on the wall.

I set my jaw. I planned my grin.  
I had my answers, hard and sly:  
“Yes, ma’am, repentance suits the cell;  
No, ma’am, I never ask you why.”

She sat, and for a minute’s space  
The warder’s keys were all the sound;  
Then, smoothing out her sober skirt,  
She glanced not up to heaven, but round.

“Have you,” she asked, “a little lad?  
Or girls? Mine will not eat their peas.  
The youngest hides them in his shoe,  
And thinks that no one ever sees.”

I stared. The sermon did not come.  
No polished thunder filled the air.  
She spoke of coughs, and sums, and shoes,  
And ribbons tangled in their hair.

She told me how her eldest reads  
With one eye shut, to show he can;  
How small hands grow, how stockings tear,  
How quickly boys turn half a man.

The cell grew strange. The bars remained,  
The bolted door, the smell of lime;  
Yet through her talk came kitchen smoke,  
A bedtime bell, a nursery rhyme.

I had a child—I did not say  
Her name at first. My throat felt rough.  
But then I asked, “Do girls of four  
Still cry when evenings get too tough?”

The lady nodded, grave and plain,  
As if I’d asked a thing worth knowing.  
“No doubt,” said she. “They cry, and then  
They fall asleep without it showing.”

No “fallen soul,” no “erring one,”  
No holy sigh, no practiced tear—  
Only two parents, for a while,  
Discussing those who were not here.

And when she left, I kept my sneer  
Prepared, but could not make it stay.  
A proper lady crossed the yard;  
A common mother went away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic monologue in verse about a villainous-looking prisoner entering a visitation room, judging the woman who came to see him, then discovering they are both simply human.
counterfactuals.output:
They bring me in with iron at my wrists,  
the old parade of monster into light—  
a door unlocked, a guard’s indifferent fist,  
the table bolted down, the window white.

I know the part. I wear it like a brand:  
the shaven skull, the scar, the sullen jaw,  
the numbers stamped in blue across my hand,  
the eyes that made the softer people draw

their children closer. Let them. I have fed  
on fear before; it sweetens in the mouth.  
I lift my chin as if the world were dead  
and I the last black tree bent from the south.

And there you sit.

Not crying. That was strange.  
No trembling cup, no saintly folded hands.  
Your face was pale, but not the face of change—  
more like a shore that understands the sands.

I judged you then. Of course I did. I thought:  
Here comes another woman dressed in grace,  
to spend an hour proving she is not  
the kind of thing that stands in such a place.

Your coat too clean. Your collar pinned too straight.  
A little cross. A little careful hair.  
The scent of rain about you, and of late  
decisions made upstairs, in kinder air.

I thought: You want confession like a key.  
You want my wickedness arranged and named,  
so you may carry home a part of me  
and say, “I saw the fire, and was not flamed.”

I thought: You want to pity, and be pure.  
To look at ruin through a pane of glass.  
To ask me if my soul has found a cure,  
then watch the hour gather up and pass.

So I sat down as thunder might sit down,  
with all its dark rehearsed within its chest;  
I dragged the chair. I let the metal drown  
whatever gentleness might have confessed.

You looked at me.

Not through me. Not above.  
Not at the wound, the record, or the chain.  
You looked as if the opposite of love  
was not my hate, but only someone’s pain.

I wanted you to flinch. I bared my teeth.  
I made my voice a cellar full of stones.  
I spoke of blood as if it were a wreath  
I’d earned by breaking other people’s bones.

And still you did not bless me or recoil.  
You did not shrink to make my shadow large.  
You only set your tired hands on the oil-  
stained table, like two boats too worn to charge

another sea.

Then quietly you said  
my name—not “prisoner,” not “case,” not “sin.”  
My name, as if it had not long been dead,  
as if some door inside had opened in.

I laughed. It cracked. I hated that it cracked.  
A laugh should be a weapon, sharp and thrown.  
But mine fell short, a common, clumsy act,  
and there we heard it lying there, a stone.

You told me why you came. Not for the tale.  
Not for my darkness mounted on your wall.  
You had a son. He, too, had gone to jail.  
You had a husband no one loved at all.

You had done harm by silence, harm by pride.  
You had looked away from bruises, bills, and need.  
You had prayed loud at church and gone outside  
to pass the hungry neighbor without heed.

And I, who built my throne from being worse,  
felt something in me lessen, then begin.  
What is a villain, stripped of stage and curse?  
A man who chose, and chose, and called it skin.

What is an angel, emptied of her light?  
A woman keeping watch beside regret.  
The room grew small. The chains grew strangely slight.  
The glass between all souls grew thinner yet.

I saw the powder gathered in your lines,  
the sleepless purple shadowing your eyes,  
the wedding ring worn narrow by designs  
that life had rubbed from gold to compromise.

You saw—God help us—past my practiced sneer:  
the boy who stole because the cupboards moaned,  
the youth who learned that mercy disappears  
when fists speak first and no one is atoned.

Not innocence. No. Do not make me clean.  
I did the things they whisper that I did.  
There is no hidden lily under green  
black water, no lost halo to unlid.

And you—no saint. Your hands were not unstained.  
They shook, and not from cold or holy awe.  
We sat there, two who had endured and pained,  
two creatures caught beneath the same dumb law:

that every heart, however caged or crowned,  
is half a hunger and half a plea;  
that every life drags shadows on the ground;  
that none of us is only what they see.

The guard coughed once. The hour started closing.  
Your chair sighed backward. Mine stayed bolted fast.  
No hymn rose up. No sudden rose imposing  
its red forgiveness on the iron past.

You left me nothing—no excuse, no creed,  
no little phrase to stitch across my shame.  
Only your eyes, which asked no man to bleed  
for show, and gave no pardon with my name.

Yet after you were gone, the room remained  
less like a cage than like a human place.  
My wrists were raw. The old fluorescent stained  
the table. Still, I touched my ruined face

as if to learn its edges were not all  
the mask men made, nor all the mask I chose.  
Somewhere beyond the concrete and the wall,  
you walked beneath the ordinary snows.

And I sat breathing—beast, and man, and child—  
with nothing solved, with nothing justified;  
no less condemned, no less unreconciled,  
but less alone in all I could not hide.

So bring me in again with iron wrists.  
Let strangers name the monster that they see.  
I know the part. The scar. The clenching fists.  
But now I know who sits across from me.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a witty, morally serious poem with Christian themes based on Matthew 25 (“I was in prison and you visited me”), showing that grace may arrive through mundane small talk rather than sermons.
counterfactuals.output:
**Small Talk at County**

I did not bring a thunderclap,  
no tract with flames in red;  
I brought two coffees, lukewarm, capped,  
and asked, “How’s your bad bed?”

He laughed. “It’s still a masterpiece  
of government design—  
a mattress thin as legal briefs,  
with all the warmth of twine.”

We spoke of weather, basketball,  
the vending machine’s sins,  
how powdered cream is not cream at all,  
how everybody wins

at checkers till they don’t. I said  
my car still made that sound.  
He said, “That’s probably just your tread—  
or doom.” We both looked down

and smiled, as if the Kingdom came  
in Styrofoam disguise,  
not robed in lightning, crowned in flame,  
but cracking jokes, small-sized.

No sermon shook the cinderblock.  
No angel split the air.  
A guard coughed. Someone checked the clock.  
God had the plastic chair.

For Christ is not impressed, I think,  
by pious words alone—  
He asks who crossed the painted brink  
to sit with flesh and bone.

“I was in prison”—not a test  
of eloquence or art,  
but whether love will be a guest  
where shame has learned its part.

So let the preacher preach, amen;  
let choirs have their hour.  
But grace may start with, “How you been?”  
and bloom, a stubborn flower.

And when the final doors swing wide,  
and all our masks are through,  
the Lord may grin and step aside:  
“You visited Me too.”
